After a precious-metals selloff: a five-step weekly review

A fast selloff invites fast opinions. A short weekly routine creates enough distance to distinguish what the market did, why it may have happened and what—if anything—you need to change.

Why a routine matters now

Late October 2026 has been difficult for precious-metals investors. Gold dropped below $4,000 during the week ending October 23, while silver and platinum also weakened. The move arrived alongside higher oil prices, renewed inflation anxiety, shifting Federal Reserve expectations and selling across risk assets.

In this environment, checking prices every few minutes can feel responsible while actually making judgment worse. Each headline offers a new story, and the emotional brain starts treating movement as information. A weekly review is not indifference. It is a way to put events in the same frame, using the same questions each time.

Step 1: measure the move before explaining it

Record the weekly close, percentage change and distance from a relevant reference point such as the 50-day average or your own purchase price. Use the same source and the same closing convention each week. Note whether you are looking at spot, futures, an ETF, a mining share or a retail bullion quote. They are related, but not interchangeable.

Also record the timestamp. GoldAlert's signal files use scheduled daily-close data, while embedded third-party charts may update differently. A stale value can create a false conclusion before analysis begins.

Step 2: check the macro trio

Review the US dollar, real yields and oil. A stronger dollar and higher real yields often pressure gold because they increase the relative appeal of dollar assets and interest-bearing securities. Higher oil can support gold through geopolitical fear, but it can also revive inflation and rate-hike expectations. Write down what happened rather than assuming the usual relationship held.

Then check the week's major central-bank communication and inflation releases. Avoid interpreting a single data point in isolation. What matters is whether the sequence of data is changing the expected policy path.

Step 3: separate physical demand from market flows

Look for ETF inflows or outflows, futures positioning and credible reports of retail or central-bank demand. Physical buying can be firm while investment funds are selling, or the reverse. The price reflects both, plus available inventory and liquidity.

Official-sector data often arrives with a delay and may be revised. Treat it as structural context, not a live trading signal. In August 2026, the World Gold Council reported 39 tonnes of net central-bank buying. That supports the idea that official demand continues, but it does not prevent a weekly selloff.

Step 4: use ratios as questions, not answers

The gold/silver ratio asks whether silver is gaining or losing relative strength. The gold/oil ratio offers a rough view of gold's purchasing power against energy. Gold-to-equity and crypto ratios can show which asset is leading. A ratio move is an invitation to investigate; it is not proof that one side is “cheap” and must reverse.

Write one sentence for each ratio you follow. For example: “The gold/silver ratio rose because silver fell faster.” That is more disciplined than jumping directly to “silver must rally.”

Step 5: return to the portfolio

End with questions only you can answer. Did the week's move push metals above or below your target allocation? Do you need cash within the next year? Has the reason for owning the position changed, or only its price? Is your physical-metal spread wider than you assumed? Would doing nothing remain consistent with your written plan?

If a position is causing panic, reduce the problem to size, time horizon and liquidity. A market forecast cannot repair an allocation that was too large from the start. Conversely, a diversified long-term allocation does not require a reaction to every difficult week.

Keep a one-page record

A useful weekly note can fit on one page: prices and timestamps, the macro trio, flow data, two ratios, and one portfolio decision. Include “no action” as a valid decision. Over time, the record will reveal whether your rules are consistent or whether headlines keep changing them.
